```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 9.5,
                     fig.height = 5, dpi = 110)
library(SimSurvey)
vignette_widget <- function(p) {
  p <- plotly::partial_bundle(p, type = "cartesian", local = FALSE)
  axes <- grep("^[xy]axis[0-9]*$", names(p$x$layout), value = TRUE)
  for (axis in axes) p$x$layout[[axis]]$automargin <- TRUE
  margins <- list(l = 80, r = 45, t = 50, b = 85)
  if (!is.null(p$x$layout$legend$y) && p$x$layout$legend$y < 0) margins$b <- 140
  p$x$layout$margin <- margins
  index <- which(vapply(p$dependencies,
    function(dependency) dependency$name == "plotly-cartesian", logical(1)))
  # Keep only the large Plotly bundle external; embed local support resources.
  p$dependencies[[index]]$script <- list(list(
    src = p$dependencies[[index]]$script, "data-external" = "1"))
  p
}
```

## Questions the new features can answer

SimSurvey now simulates multiple fisheries with user-supplied allocations,
fishery monitoring, and independent survey programs. Weight and maturity models
add biomass and mature-biomass truth. These extensions support questions about
how targeting, knowledge, gear selectivity, reporting, and biological sampling
affect catches, CPUE, and survey data. For population generation and stratified
survey analysis, see [Regular et al. (2020)](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0232822).

Fisheries allocate deaths already specified by total mortality `Z`. They do not
change subsequent years' populations. Surveys observe the original annual
population, including when simulated after fisheries.

```{r workflow, echo=FALSE, fig.height=3.4, fig.cap="Fisheries and surveys start from the same annual population. Outputs retain their fishery or survey-program identifiers."}
par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
plot.new()
plot.window(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1), xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i")
box_text <- function(x, y, w, h, title, body) {
  rect(x - w / 2, y - h / 2, x + w / 2, y + h / 2,
       col = "#EDF3F7", border = "#52758C", lwd = 1.2)
  text(x, y + h / 2 - 0.075, title, font = 2, cex = 0.85)
  text(x, y - 0.045, body, cex = 0.8)
}
box_text(0.165, 0.5, 0.31, 0.64, "Population and biology",
         "sim_abundance()\nAbundance, mortality,\ngrowth, weight, maturity\n\nsim_distribution()\nSpatial distribution")
box_text(0.515, 0.75, 0.285, 0.30, "sim_fisheries()", "Fishing and monitoring")
box_text(0.515, 0.25, 0.285, 0.30, "sim_surveys()", "Independent survey programs")
box_text(0.865, 0.5, 0.25, 0.46, "Simulated data", "for analysis\n\nCatch, effort and\nbiological samples")
segments(c(0.32, 0.345, 0.6575, 0.6575, 0.695),
         c(0.5, 0.25, 0.75, 0.25, 0.25),
         c(0.345, 0.345, 0.695, 0.695, 0.695),
         c(0.5, 0.75, 0.75, 0.25, 0.75), col = "#52758C")
arrows(c(0.345, 0.345, 0.695), c(0.75, 0.25, 0.5),
       c(0.3725, 0.3725, 0.74), c(0.75, 0.25, 0.5),
       length = 0.065, col = "#52758C")
```

## Population and biological relationships

The setup follows the `sim_survey()` example: five ages, a 20-km grid, and
default population and spatial processes, extended to ten years. One population
is shared by every example. It is illustrative, not a reconstruction of 3Ps cod.

```{r population}
set.seed(601)
population <- sim_abundance(ages = 1:5, years = 2001:2010) |>
  sim_distribution(grid = make_grid(res = c(20, 20)))
```

`sim_abundance()` accepts growth, weight, and maturity functions.
`sim_growth()` is an alias for `sim_vonB()`. `sim_weight()` returns kilograms
from length in centimetres; `sim_maturity()` returns maturity probabilities.
Its default basis is length; use `maturity_by = "age"` with age-appropriate
parameters for an age-based curve.

Weight defaults follow [Varkey et al. (2024), Table 10](https://publications.gc.ca/collections/collection_2024/mpo-dfo/Fs97-13-1381-eng.pdf).
Maturity defaults approximate the historical 3Ps female relationship in
[Brattey and Morgan (1996), Table 3](https://waves-vagues.dfo-mpo.gc.ca/Library/198884.pdf).
Here one curve applies to all fish; these are starting values, not a contemporary
sex-specific assessment model. For example, `maturity = sim_maturity(x50 = 50)`
changes the length with 50% maturity probability.

```{r biology-curves, echo=FALSE, fig.height=4.5}
length_cm <- 0:100
weight_curve <- plotly::plot_ly(x = length_cm, y = sim_weight()(length_cm),
  type = "scatter", mode = "lines", name = "Weight") |>
  plotly::layout(xaxis = list(title = "Length (cm)"), yaxis = list(title = "Weight (kg)"))
maturity_curve <- plotly::plot_ly(x = length_cm, y = sim_maturity()(length_cm),
  type = "scatter", mode = "lines", name = "Maturity probability") |>
  plotly::layout(xaxis = list(title = "Length (cm)"), yaxis = list(title = "Maturity probability"))
plotly::subplot(weight_curve, maturity_curve, titleX = TRUE, titleY = TRUE, margin = 0.09) |>
  plotly::layout(showlegend = FALSE) |> vignette_widget()
```

`B` and `S` contain expected biomass and mature biomass in kilograms, by age
and year. `B_at_length` and `S_at_length` give the corresponding length-based
values; `sp_N` contains spatial `B` and `S`. `S` covers all fish under the
supplied curve, without sex structure, spawning timing, or recruitment feedback.
Both summaries integrate weight and maturity jointly over the length-age key
([Appendix A1](#biology-equations)).

```{r biomass-trends, fig.height=4.5}
plotly::subplot(plot_trend(population, mat = "B"), plot_trend(population, mat = "S"),
                titleX = TRUE, titleY = TRUE, margin = 0.09) |>
  plotly::layout(showlegend = FALSE) |> vignette_widget()
```

## Multiple fisheries and their allocations

Omitting `sim` from `sim_fishery()` creates a configuration without simulation
or random draws. Declare fisheries together; their names identify the outputs.

```{r configurations}
trawl <- sim_fishery(fishery_share = 0.2, catch_model = sim_capture(q = 400))
gillnet <- sim_fishery(
  fishery_share = 0.1, catch_model = sim_capture(q = 200),
  selectivity = sim_logistic(x50 = 40), selectivity_by = "length"
)

set.seed(502)
fished <- population |>
  sim_fisheries(trawl = trawl, gillnet = gillnet, n_sims = 5)
```

The trawl uses default age selectivity; the gillnet illustrates length selectivity.
These names do not imply calibrated gear models. To run one fishery directly,
use `sim_fishery(population, fishery_share = 0.2, catch_model = sim_capture(q = 400))`.

`sim_capture()` converts its `q` coefficient, gear amount, duration, selectivity,
and cell area to an encounter probability. Capture `q` has grid-area units per
gear-time unit and can exceed one; survey `q` is a dimensionless probability.
Default gear amount and duration are one, and their product is effort. Specify
`gear_unit` and `time_unit` for physical units. Both components can be callbacks;
`capacity_per_gear` adds a catch-capacity limit. Every fishery inherits the
population's weight relationship.

`fishery_share` allocates a share of `Z` **before selectivity**. Selectivity
is not rescaled: its magnitude affects both the reference catch target and
capture. Targets are total numbers of fish, not kilogram TACs. Combined shares
and selectivity must fit `Z` at every age/year; incompatible allocations error.

Operations from active fisheries are interleaved at random on shared stocks.
Accepted catches reduce available fish and age-specific death allowances.
This prevents double removals but can constrain individual allocations.

| Component in `fishery` | Contents |
|:---|:---|
| `annual` | Target, catch, effort, CPUE, shortfall, and stopping status |
| `setdet` | Operations, reports, sampling counts, and constraint flags |
| `catch_at_age`, `catch_at_length` | True aggregate catch composition |
| `sp_removals`, `mortality_ledger` | Spatial removals and the shared population balance |
| `reference` | Reference and realized catches and F at age, original N/Z, and `total_deaths` |
| `samp` | Biological observations and sampling probabilities |

Commercial catches remain aggregate; only bounded biological samples become
individual records. `light = FALSE` retains joint age-length catches and sample
truth for inspection.

### Shortfalls and mortality

A **shortfall** is the integer catch target minus realized catch.
`target_met` means the target was caught; `exhausted` means no eligible
accessible catching opportunities remain; `operation_limit` means the allowed
operations ended first. Access restrictions, gear response, and shared stocks
can all constrain catches.

For 100 fish, `Z = log(2)`, full selectivity, and share 0.4, the target is
20 fish from 50 total deaths. If only five are caught, the shortfall is 15.
Reference F is \(0.4\log(2)\simeq0.277\); realized-equivalent F is
\((5/100)\log(2)/(1-0.5)\simeq0.069\). The remaining balance is 45 other deaths
and 50 survivors. Unused fishing allocation becomes other deaths under fixed
mortality; it does not improve later survival.

`total_deaths` is the rounded all-cause death count for an age/year, shared
across fisheries and repeated on their reference rows. Do not sum it across
fisheries. `F_realized` is the Baranov-equivalent rate from true catches,
original `N`, and fixed `Z`. Meeting a total-number target need not reproduce
reference F at every age. [Appendix A2](#fishery-targets)
defines rounding and zero-abundance cases.

## Fishing locations and CPUE

`targeting = 0` gives **random fishing**: each operation draws an accessible
cell with equal probability, allowing repeated visits and zero catches.
Default `targeting = 1` favors high vulnerable density and mixes in 5% random
exploration. Density updates after catches.

Default `knowledge_sd = 0` gives accurate knowledge. Positive values add map
error, scaled to initial mean vulnerable density. Errors are redrawn each year
and held across its operations. Fisheries therefore follow current-year
distributions, without a lagged map, learning, or vessel routing.

```{r targeting-map, fig.height=6.5}
plot_fishery(fished, "trawl", which_year = 2005, which_sim = NULL) |> vignette_widget()
```

The map counts operations, including unsuccessful ones. The other panels compare
true catch composition with unweighted biological samples. Annual catch and its
integer target can be viewed with `plot_fishery_trend()`:

```{r fishery-trends, fig.height=4.5}
plot_fishery_trend(fished, "trawl", metric = "n") |> vignette_widget()
```

### Comparing random and targeted fishing

We use full selectivity to remove age composition as a cause of changing
catchability. Both scenarios use `knowledge_sd = 0.25`: map-error SD is one
quarter of initial mean vulnerable density. Knowledge is useful but imperfect.
Random fishing ignores that signal. Only targeting differs; reporting and
biological monitoring are held fixed.

```{r cpue-fishing}
run_cpue <- function(targeting) {
  set.seed(602)
  sim_fishery(population,
    fishery_share = 0.2, catch_model = sim_capture(q = 1),
    selectivity = function(age) 1, targeting = targeting, knowledge_sd = 0.25,
    max_operations = 30, sampling_coverage = 0, n_sims = 5)
}
cpue_scenarios <- list("Random fishing" = run_cpue(0), "Targeted fishing" = run_cpue(1))
```

These deliberately effort-limited runs stop at 30 operations per year, below
their allocations, without quota or mortality capping. They retain shortfalls.
With `q = 1` and 400-square-kilometre cells, encounter probability is low.
Biological monitoring is disabled.

```{r cpue-summary}
cpue_summary <- data.table::rbindlist(lapply(names(cpue_scenarios), function(label) {
  result <- cpue_scenarios[[label]]
  summary <- result$fishery$annual[, list(cpue = sum(n) / sum(effort)), by = "year"]
  summary$scenario <- label
  summary$N <- colSums(result$N)[match(summary$year, result$years)]
  summary$relative_cpue <- summary$cpue / mean(summary$cpue)
  summary$relative_N <- summary$N / mean(summary$N)
  summary
}))
```

```{r cpue-comparison, echo=FALSE, fig.height=5.5}
abundance <- cpue_summary[scenario == "Random fishing", ]
trajectory <- plotly::plot_ly(x = abundance$year, y = abundance$relative_N,
  type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers", name = "Abundance", legendgroup = "N",
  line = list(color = "black"), marker = list(color = "black", size = 6)) |>
  plotly::layout(xaxis = list(title = "Year"), yaxis = list(title = "Series / overall mean"))
limit <- 1.05 * max(cpue_summary$relative_N, cpue_summary$relative_cpue)
proportionality <- plotly::plot_ly(x = c(0, limit), y = c(0, limit),
  type = "scatter", mode = "lines", name = "Proportional", line = list(color = "grey50", dash = "dash")) |>
  plotly::layout(xaxis = list(title = "Abundance / overall mean"), yaxis = list(title = "CPUE / overall mean"))
colours <- c("Random fishing" = "#0072B2", "Targeted fishing" = "#D55E00")
for (label in names(cpue_scenarios)) {
  keep <- cpue_summary$scenario == label
  values <- cpue_summary[keep, ]
  trajectory <- trajectory |> plotly::add_trace(x = values$year, y = values$relative_cpue,
    type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers", name = label, legendgroup = label,
    line = list(color = colours[[label]]), marker = list(color = colours[[label]], size = 6),
    inherit = FALSE)
  proportionality <- proportionality |> plotly::add_trace(x = values$relative_N, y = values$relative_cpue,
    text = paste0("Year: ", values$year, "<br>N: ", round(values$N), "<br>CPUE: ", round(values$cpue, 1)),
    hoverinfo = "text", type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers", name = label,
    legendgroup = label, showlegend = FALSE, line = list(color = colours[[label]]),
    marker = list(color = colours[[label]], size = 6), inherit = FALSE)
}
plotly::subplot(trajectory, proportionality, titleX = TRUE, titleY = TRUE, margin = 0.09) |>
  plotly::layout(legend = list(orientation = "h", y = -0.25)) |> vignette_widget()
```

Each series is divided by its **overall mean across years**. CPUE is annual
total true catch divided by total effort, pooled across five conditional
replicates before scaling. Scaling compares trajectories, not absolute catch rates.

Targeted fishing responds to concentration as well as total abundance. Random
fishing is proportional to abundance in expectation before depletion, but a
finite number of operations over a patchy grid produces sampling variation.
Preferential fishing need not produce hyperstability: changing concentration
can make CPUE decline more slowly or more quickly than abundance. Moving an
otherwise unchanged spatial pattern need not break proportionality when
harvesters can follow it ([Appendix A10](#cpue-proportionality)).

More effort cannot independently increase the fixed annual catch budget.
A quota-capped final operation retains its specified effort, so its CPUE is
quota-limited. Use total catch divided by total effort, retain zero catches,
and keep fisheries with different effort units separate. CPUE standardization
is left to downstream analysis.

## Fishery reporting and biological sampling

Reporting defaults to unbiased totals without error, and every operation is
selected for biological monitoring up to the length and age caps.
The comparisons below reduce coverage, change selection at that same coverage,
or introduce reporting error. The helper repeats the same fishing configuration
and seed.

```{r monitoring-comparisons}
run_fleets <- function(trawl_spec) {
  set.seed(502)
  sim_fisheries(population, trawl = trawl_spec, gillnet = gillnet, n_sims = 5)
}
random_monitoring <- run_fleets(modifyList(trawl, list(sampling_coverage = 0.25)))
preferential_monitoring <- run_fleets(modifyList(trawl,
  list(sampling_coverage = 0.25, sampling_targeting = 2)))
under_reporting <- run_fleets(modifyList(trawl,
  list(reporting_factor = 0.8, reporting_cv = 0.2)))
```

`reporting_factor` and `reporting_cv` set the mean and CV of an operation's
lognormal reporting multiplier, applied to both numbers and kilograms.
Biological samples come from true catches, regardless of reports.

Coverage is an **expected proportion**, not a fixed count. Positive
`sampling_targeting` favors operations with larger reported catches while
preserving that expected coverage.

```{r monitoring-figure, echo=FALSE, fig.height=5.5}
annual <- under_reporting$fishery$annual[under_reporting$fishery$annual$fishery == "trawl", ]
limits <- range(c(annual$n, annual$reported_n)) / 1000
reporting <- plotly::plot_ly(x = annual$n / 1000, y = annual$reported_n / 1000,
  type = "scatter", mode = "markers", name = "Reports", showlegend = FALSE) |>
  plotly::add_lines(x = limits, y = limits, inherit = FALSE, name = "Identity",
    line = list(color = "grey50", dash = "dash"), showlegend = FALSE) |>
  plotly::layout(xaxis = list(title = "True catch (1000 fish)"),
    yaxis = list(title = "Reported catch (1000 fish)"))
truth <- fished$fishery$catch_at_length
truth <- truth[truth$fishery == "trawl", list(n = sum(n)), by = "length"]
truth <- truth[order(truth$length), ]
measured_frequency <- function(result) {
  sample <- result$fishery$samp
  count <- table(factor(sample$length[sample$fishery == "trawl"], levels = truth$length))
  as.numeric(count / sum(count))
}
composition <- plotly::plot_ly(x = truth$length, y = truth$n / sum(truth$n),
  type = "scatter", mode = "lines", name = "Catch truth", line = list(color = "black")) |>
  plotly::add_lines(y = measured_frequency(random_monitoring), name = "Uniform monitoring",
    line = list(color = "#0072B2", dash = "dash")) |>
  plotly::add_lines(y = measured_frequency(preferential_monitoring), name = "Preferential monitoring",
    line = list(color = "#D55E00", dash = "dot")) |>
  plotly::layout(xaxis = list(title = "Length group (cm)"), yaxis = list(title = "Proportion"))
plotly::subplot(reporting, composition, titleX = TRUE, titleY = TRUE, margin = 0.09) |>
  plotly::layout(legend = list(orientation = "h", y = -0.25)) |> vignette_widget()
```

The left panel shows reports against true catches. The right compares pooled
catch truth with unweighted measured-length compositions at 25% coverage.
These are descriptive proportions, not catch-composition estimates. Even random
operation selection with fixed fish-sampling caps can overrepresent fish from
small catches. Known probabilities support appropriate weighting; zero coverage
and convenience sampling pose different problems.

### Maturity observations

`maturity_sampling = "aged"` examines every aged fish; `"measured"` examines
every length-measured fish; `"none"` collects no maturity observations.
For example:

```{r maturity-observations, eval=FALSE}
sim_fishery(population, fishery_share = 0.2,
  catch_model = sim_capture(q = 400), maturity_sampling = "measured")
```

`mature` is binary, with `NA` for unexamined fish. `maturity_observed` marks
examinations and `n_maturity` counts them. Latent states are drawn for every
measured fish before the protocol masks observations, so changing only this
setting preserves catches, existing samples, and overlapping maturity states.
Classification is perfect; individual maturation histories and sex-specific
biology are outside this model.

## Independent survey programs

Survey configurations also omit `sim`. Allocation, gear dimensions, and
biological sample sizes use their defaults here: 160 sets per year and replicate
on this grid. The second program changes catchability to a length-based curve.

```{r surveys}
set.seed(503)
programs <- fished |>
  sim_surveys(
    survey_A = sim_survey(),
    survey_B = sim_survey(q = sim_logistic(x50 = 40), q_by = "length")
  )
selected <- programs |> select_survey("survey_B") |> run_strat() |> strat_error()
```

Both programs sample the original rounded annual population independently.
They do not deplete each other's stocks or consume fishery mortality.
Program-specific availability and observations are stored in `survey_programs`;
common population data are stored once. `select_survey()` creates a standard
single-survey view for existing analysis and plotting functions.

```{r survey-comparison, echo=FALSE, fig.height=5.5}
survey_figures <- lapply(names(programs$survey_programs), function(label) {
  view <- programs |> select_survey(label) |> run_strat() |> strat_error()
  estimate <- view$total_strat_error
  plotly::plot_ly(x = estimate$year, y = estimate$I_hat / 1e6,
    type = "scatter", mode = "markers", name = paste(label, "estimates")) |>
    plotly::add_lines(x = view$years, y = colSums(view$I) / 1e6, inherit = FALSE,
      name = paste(label, "availability"), line = list(color = "black")) |>
    plotly::layout(xaxis = list(title = "Year"), yaxis = list(title = "Available fish (millions)"))
})
plotly::subplot(survey_figures, titleX = TRUE, titleY = TRUE, margin = 0.09) |>
  plotly::layout(legend = list(orientation = "h", y = -0.25)) |> vignette_widget()
```

Each program's estimates target its own availability `I`, rather than total
abundance `N`. Adding `B` and `S` truth does not add biomass estimators to
`run_strat()`. Survey graphics work on the selected view:

```{r survey-view, fig.height=6.5}
plot_survey(selected, which_year = 2005, which_sim = 1) |> vignette_widget()
```

Survey `samp$weight` gives kilograms for every caught fish; `setdet$kg` and
`samp_totals$kg_caught` sum all catches, not just measured fish.
`full_setdet$kg` retains set/age totals with `light = FALSE`.
Unmeasured weights are latent truth, without measurement error.

Use `samp[samp$measured, ]` for observed survey lengths and
`samp[samp$aged, ]` for observed ages. Fishery `samp` contains only measured
fish, with unobserved ages missing. Both use `maturity_observed`.
Keep program identifiers when combining records; survey set identifiers are
program-scoped. Stratified fishery age caps apply per operation/length group,
whereas survey caps use `age_space_group` per replicate/year/length group.

## Scope and reproducibility

These five fishing/observation replicates share one population history.
For independent biological histories, repeat population generation in an outer
loop. Matching replicate IDs do not identify common individual fish across programs.

All fishing truth precedes monitoring; all survey-program truth precedes
biological subsampling. Monitoring settings therefore preserve fishing truth.
Names are processed in canonical order, but adding or renaming programs can
change random draws. Record seeds and settings: a shared seed makes each scenario
reproducible, without guaranteeing paired random innovations.

All fishery catches are retained. Discards, trip/port hierarchies, vessel routes,
seasons, and population feedback are not represented. Custom capture functions
can replace `sim_capture()`: they receive aggregate available age-length counts,
selectivity, cell area, and operation details, and return bounded whole-fish
proposals, with zero at zero selectivity.

## Backwards compatibility

Attach biological relationships to an older distributed object, then refresh
summaries without regenerating its trajectory:

```{r migration, eval=FALSE}
sim$sim_weight <- sim_weight()
sim$sim_maturity <- sim_maturity()
sim$maturity_by <- "length"
sim <- round_sim(sim)
```

For an abundance-only object, attach the relationships before `sim_distribution()`.
Number-only legacy surveys can use `maturity_sampling = "none"`; missing weight
models give missing positive-catch kilograms and zero kilograms for empty catches.
Defaults are not silently installed.

Growth remains stored as `sim_length`. Fishery-level `weight` arguments were
removed before release. Prefer `x50` to deprecated `x0`; positional logistic
calls keep their meaning. `death_budget` remains an alias for `total_deaths`.

Older multi-year fishery outputs affected by the annual-stock selection defect
must be rerun from saved populations. Do not patch their ledgers or regenerate
the population trajectory; `sim_fisheries()` replaces fishery results from the
original annual snapshots.

## Appendix A: mathematics of the extensions

This appendix starts from generated abundance, mortality, the length-age key,
and the grid. Population generation and stratified estimation follow the original paper.

### Notation and units

| Symbol | Meaning |
|:---|:---|
| \(a,l,y,c,f,r,j\) | Age, length group, year, cell, fishery, replicate, operation |
| \(N_{a,y}, n_{c,a,l}^{(j)}\) | Rounded annual abundance and remaining integer stock |
| \(P_{l,a}=P(l\mid a)\) | Growth-model length-age probabilities; columns sum to one |
| \(w_l,m_{a,l}\) | Kilograms per fish and maturity probability |
| \(p_{f,y},s_{f,a,l}\) | Fishery share and selectivity probabilities |
| \(A_c,G_j,T_j,E_j\) | Cell area, gear amount, duration, and nominal effort \(G_jT_j\) |
| \(q_f,q_{s,l}\) | Capture area per gear-time, and dimensionless survey catchability |
| \(\beta_f,\sigma_f,\epsilon_f\) | Targeting, knowledge-error multiplier, exploration |
| \(\pi_j,\pi_{L\mid j},\pi_{A\mid L,j}\) | Operation and conditional biological selection probabilities |

Omitted indices are held fixed. Biological functions are deterministic and
constant across cells and years. Population summaries use the growth key's
discrete length labels. Age-selective surveys retain their continuous growth
draws followed by length rounding, so the key discretizes that relationship.

### A1. Weight, maturity, biomass, and mature biomass {#biology-equations}

The default functions are

\[
w_l=\alpha l^b,\quad \alpha=10^{-5.2106},\quad b=3.0879,
\qquad m(x)=\operatorname{logit}^{-1}\{k(x-x_{50})\}.
\]

Weight uses centimetres and kilograms. Default maturity uses \(k=0.28\)
per centimetre and \(x_{50}=47.81\) cm. For length-based maturity,
\(m_{a,l}=m(l)\); for age-based maturity, \(m_{a,l}=m(a)\).

\[
B_{a,y}=N_{a,y}\sum_lP_{l,a}w_l,\qquad
S_{a,y}=N_{a,y}\sum_lP_{l,a}w_lm_{a,l},
\]
\[
B_{l,y}=w_l\sum_aN_{a,y}P_{l,a},\qquad
S_{l,y}=w_l\sum_aN_{a,y}P_{l,a}m_{a,l}.
\]

Annual totals match across age and length representations, with \(0\le S\le B\).
Spatial summaries use the same conditional expectations and refresh after
abundance rounding. No spawning timing, female fraction, or fecundity is applied.

As a hand calculation, suppose an age group contains 100 fish, with probabilities
0.75 and 0.25 of lengths whose weights are 1 and 8 kg and maturities 0 and 1.
Biomass is \(100(0.75+0.25\times8)=275\) kg; mature biomass is
\(100(0.25\times8)=200\) kg. Multiplying biomass by mean maturity instead gives
only \(275\times0.25=68.75\) kg. Converting an age-based mass matrix with the
ordinary number-based length-age key would likewise lose the relevant association.

### A2. Reference catches and integer mortality budgets {#fishery-targets}

Mean selectivity at age and reference fishing mortality are

\[
\bar s_{f,a}=\sum_lP_{l,a}s_{f,a,l},\qquad
F^{\mathrm{ref}}_{f,a,y}=p_{f,y}Z_{a,y}\bar s_{f,a}.
\]

For constant annual mortality, the
[Baranov reference catch](https://www.fao.org/4/X9026E/x9026e06.htm) becomes

\[
C^{\mathrm{ref}}_{f,a,y}
=N_{a,y}\frac{F^{\mathrm{ref}}_{f,a,y}}{Z_{a,y}}(1-e^{-Z_{a,y}})
=N_{a,y}p_{f,y}\bar s_{f,a}(1-e^{-Z_{a,y}}).
\]

The final expression defines zero catch at \(Z=0\), without division by zero.
The constraint is \(\sum_f p_{f,y}\bar s_{f,a}\le1\) for every age/year
(up to floating-point tolerance). These are reference quantities: realized age
composition and implied allocation of deaths may differ.

Cell abundances are rounded with R's `round()` convention and annual abundance
is recomputed from cells. Within each cell/age, integer length stocks are drawn
as a multinomial allocation of that cell count with probabilities \(P_{l,a}\).
They are independent allocations in each replicate/year, not tracked individuals.

Define balanced rounding \(\mathcal R(\mathbf x)\) by flooring each value and
adding one to the largest fractional remainders until the total is
`round(sum(x))`. R uses ties-to-even for half-integer totals; remainder ties use
age order or canonical fishery-name order. Then

\[
\mathbf D_y=\mathcal R\{N_{a,y}(1-e^{-Z_{a,y}})\}_a,\qquad
\mathbf Q_y=\mathcal R\{\sum_a C^{\mathrm{ref}}_{f,a,y}\}_f.
\]

\(D_{a,y}\), stored as `total_deaths`, is the shared whole-fish count of all
deaths at age, including fishing and other deaths. \(Q_{f,y}\) is one fishery's
total-number target. Target rounding is joint across fisheries, not independent rounding
of each age/fishery catch. The valid combined target cannot exceed the overall
death budget; realized catches must additionally fit age-specific budgets.

After fishing, retain true catches and their mortality equivalents at age:

\[
U^{\mathrm{realized}}_{f,a,y}=\frac{C^{\mathrm{realized}}_{f,a,y}}{N_{a,y}},\qquad
F^{\mathrm{realized}}_{f,a,y}=U^{\mathrm{realized}}_{f,a,y}
\frac{Z_{a,y}}{1-e^{-Z_{a,y}}}.
\]

For positive N and zero Z, realized catches and F are zero. At zero N, both
realized rates are missing. The factor uses `-expm1(-Z)` for numerical stability.
No operation-time hazard is fitted and no future abundance is changed. Integer
rounding can give a death budget above the continuous expectation, so combined
equivalent F may exceed Z in tiny populations; values are retained without clipping.

### A3. Location probabilities and knowledge errors

Within a replicate/year, initial vulnerable density defines a persistent map
error for each fishery/cell. On accessible cells, let

\[
d^{(0)}_{f,c}=A_c^{-1}\sum_{a,l}n^{(0)}_{c,a,l}s_{f,a,l},\qquad
e_{f,c}\sim N\{0,(\sigma_f\overline d^{(0)}_f)^2\}.
\]

Errors are drawn once and reused across operations, with the mean taken over
accessible cells. Current density excludes ages with exhausted death budgets:

\[
d^{(j)}_{f,c}=A_c^{-1}\sum_{a,l}n^{(j)}_{c,a,l}s_{f,a,l}
\mathbf1(D^{\mathrm{remaining}}_a>0),\qquad
u^{(j)}_{f,c}=\max(0,d^{(j)}_{f,c}+e_{f,c})^{\beta_f}.
\]

For \(K_f\) accessible cells, the location probability is

\[
P(c\mid f,j)=(1-\epsilon_f)
\frac{u^{(j)}_{f,c}}{\sum_{c'}u^{(j)}_{f,c'}}+\frac{\epsilon_f}{K_f}.
\]

Zero targeting or an all-zero signal gives uniform probabilities. All accessible
cells remain in this location frame, including cells that can produce zero
catches. A fishery is exhausted when no accessible vulnerable stock has remaining
age mortality, even though the signal may suggest otherwise. Noisy knowledge
with zero targeting does not change the uniform choice probabilities.

### A4. Capture proposals, thinning, and interleaving

For a selected cell, the built-in proposal probability and counts are

\[
v_{a,l,j}=1-\exp\left(-q_fG_jT_js_{f,a,l}/A_c\right),\qquad
X_{a,l,j}\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n^{(j)}_{c,a,l},v_{a,l,j}).
\]

The engine thins proposals without replacement, first for capacity
\(\lfloor\texttt{capacity\_per\_gear}\,G_j\rfloor\), then within each age for
remaining mortality, and finally across accepted proposals for the remaining
fishery target. With category counts \(\mathbf x\), thinning to \(h\) fish uses
the multivariate hypergeometric distribution; counts are not expanded into fish.
Accepted catches reduce the common stock and age death budgets.

The capture probability describes a proposal, not the final constrained catch
distribution. `mortality_limited` and `quota_limited` flag their respective
constraints. All specified \(E_j=G_jT_j\) remains when the quota caps a catch.

One replicate/year follows this algorithm:

1. Initialize stocks, death budgets, and every fishery target once.
2. Choose the next active fishery uniformly; check its opportunities and operation limit.
3. Choose a location, resolve gear/time, propose catches, and apply constraints.
4. Update shared stock/budgets and retain the operation, including a zero catch.
5. Retire completed/exhausted/limited fisheries and repeat until none is active.
6. Allocate other deaths, then complete reporting and biological samples.

The known impossible built-in cases (`q = 0` or zero capacity) retire as exhausted.
A custom model returning zeros can instead reach its operation limit, because
the engine cannot infer all future responses of an arbitrary callback.

### A5. Residual mortality and conservation

After fishing, residual deaths at age are

\[
O_a=D_a-\sum_{f,c,l}C_{f,c,a,l}.
\]

Sample those deaths without replacement among all remaining fish at that age,
across cells and lengths. For every ledger row,

\[
n^{(0)}_{c,a,l}=\sum_f C_{f,c,a,l}+O_{c,a,l}+V_{c,a,l},
\]

where \(V\) denotes survivors. Integer stocks balance exactly. Population `B`
and `S` integrate over the length key, whereas each fishery replicate has a
particular integer length allocation; their starting masses need not be identical.
None of these deaths is subtracted again from a future pre-generated population.

### A6. Reporting and preferential monitoring

For mean reporting factor \(b\) and CV \(c\), draw independent operation multipliers

\[
\sigma_R^2=\log(1+c^2),\qquad
\log R_j\sim N(\log b-\sigma_R^2/2,\sigma_R^2).
\]

Thus \(E(R_j)=b\). Reported numbers and kilograms equal their true values times
the same \(R_j\). At zero CV the multiplier is constant; at zero mean it is zero.

Within each fishery/replicate/year, operation weights use reported catch \(r_j\):

\[
w_j=(1+r_j/\overline r)^\gamma,\qquad
\pi_j=\min(1,\lambda w_j),\qquad
\sum_j\pi_j=\texttt{sampling\_coverage}\times J.
\]

\(\gamma\) is `sampling_targeting`. Zero targeting or all-zero reported catches
gives equal probabilities. Selection is independent Bernoulli with these
probabilities, so realized coverage varies. The implementation rescales weights
for numerical stability and retains a positive numerical floor under extreme
preferences. Coverage zero and one are handled directly.

For a selected operation with catch \(C_j\), measure
\(n_{L,j}=\min(C_j,\texttt{lengths\_cap})\) fish without replacement. The
conditional length-selection probability is \(n_{L,j}/C_j\). Random age sampling
selects up to `ages_cap` from these fish. Stratified sampling selects up to that
cap within each measured length group, per operation. The conditional probability
within an age-sampling group is its selected count divided by its measured count.
Zero coverage or caps disable the corresponding observations.

Recorded probabilities describe the stages conditional on the realized frame
and previous sample. Their product is a multistage selection factor; it is not
automatically the unconditional marginal inclusion probability when later groups
depend on earlier random samples. Appropriate inference also needs a defined
estimand, frame, and positive coverage. No catch-composition estimator is supplied
by this vignette.

### A7. Maturity observations

After every existing sample is generated, draw a latent state for each measured
fish \(i\):

\[
M_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}\{m(x_i)\},\qquad
x_i=l_i\ \text{or}\ a_i.
\]

Use the simulated true age internally when maturity depends on age, even if it
will not be observed. The observation indicator is `aged`, `measured`, or zero
according to `maturity_sampling`. Report \(M_i\) when examined and `NA` otherwise.
Latent draws occur even for `"none"` when a model is present, so protocol changes
preserve overlapping states and RNG consumption. Only the bounded measured
sample is materialized for fisheries; no individual commercial-population
maturity records are needed to calculate expected `S`.

### A8. Length-selective survey observations

For length catchability \(q_{s,l}\), program-specific availability is

\[
\overline q_{s,a}=\sum_lP_{l,a}q_{s,l},\qquad
I_{s,a,y}=N_{a,y}\overline q_{s,a},\qquad
I_{s,l,y}=q_{s,l}\sum_aN_{a,y}P_{l,a}.
\]

Caught lengths conditional on age follow
\(P(l\mid a,\text{caught},s)=P_{l,a}q_{s,l}/\overline q_{s,a}\).
At zero availability there is no catch, so that conditional distribution is
never sampled. The historical age-based path uses age catchability and the
original growth sampler. New length-based draws use the growth key's labels.

Survey catches at age use binomial trials with rounded cell abundance divided
by the number of sets in that cell, and probability
\((A_{\mathrm{tow}}/A_c)\overline q_{s,a}\). Repeated-cell handling retains that
historical splitting convention; it is not fishery-style sequential depletion.
`binom_error = FALSE` rounds the corresponding expectation. Swept-area and
catchability settings must define valid probabilities. Length caps apply per
set; stratified survey age caps use `age_space_group` per replicate/year/length
group, while random caps apply per set.

For every realized caught fish i, deterministic weight is \(w(l_i)\). Catch mass
for set j is \(K_j=\sum_{i\in j}w(l_i)\), including unmeasured fish; set/age and
replicate/year totals sum the same realized weights. These are not population
biomass expectations or estimates scaled from the measured subsample. Legacy
objects without a weight model retain missing individual weights and nonempty
catch masses, with mass zero for an empty catch.

### A9. Biomass catches, CPUE, and random sequencing

With realized joint catches \(C_{j,a,l}\), operation biomass is
\(K_j=\sum_{a,l}C_{j,a,l}w_l\). Population weights apply to every fishery.
For a fishery/replicate/year,

\[
\operatorname{CPUE}=\frac{\sum_j C_j}{\sum_j E_j},\qquad
\operatorname{CPUE}_{\mathrm{biomass}}=\frac{\sum_j K_j}{\sum_j E_j}.
\]

Reported versions use reported totals. Zero total effort gives missing CPUE;
zero catches with positive effort give zero CPUE. Biomass is stored in kilograms,
even when figures display tonnes. Different fisheries' effort is not pooled.

All fisheries' truth across replicates/years is generated before reporting and
biological sampling. Survey programs likewise generate all their truth before
biological subsampling. Maturity follows every existing sample in its batch.
Names are processed canonically, and all draws use the caller's RNG state.
Changing earlier pipeline stages can still change later stages' RNG state;
repeat a stage from an explicit seed when constructing controlled comparisons.


### A10. Spatial preferences and CPUE proportionality {#cpue-proportionality}


For the plotted comparison, first pool each year's catch and effort across
replicates, giving \(H_{f,y}=\sum_r C_{f,r,y}/\sum_r E_{f,r,y}\).
For Y years, the scaled series are

\[
\widetilde H_{f,y}=\frac{H_{f,y}}{Y^{-1}\sum_{y'}H_{f,y'}},
\qquad
\widetilde N_y=\frac{N_y}{Y^{-1}\sum_{y'}N_{y'}}.
\]

Each series has temporal mean one; its first value need not be one.
The line \(\widetilde H=\widetilde N\) represents proportional trajectories
after scaling, not equal absolute catch rates.


Consider the example's equal-area cells, full selectivity, constant
effort E, and inactive capacity/quota/mortality constraints. Before depletion,
let \(n_c\) be abundance in cell c and \(N=\sum_c n_c\). With constant encounter
probability \(v=1-\exp(-q_fE/A_c)\), expected first-operation CPUE is

\[
E(C/E)=\frac{v}{E}\sum_c\pi_c n_c.
\]

Random fishing in K accessible cells gives \(vN/(EK)\). In the special case
of accurate density targeting with exploration \(\epsilon\), the expectation is

\[
E(C/E)=\frac{v}{E}\left\{(1-\epsilon)\frac{\sum_c n_c^2}{N}
+\epsilon\frac{N}{K}\right\}.
\]

With imperfect knowledge, let \(h_c=\max(0,n_c/A_c+e_c)\), using the
replicate/year's errors from A3. For positive total signal and `targeting = 1`,

\[
E(C/E\mid\mathbf e)=\frac{v}{E}\left\{(1-\epsilon)
\frac{\sum_c n_ch_c}{\sum_c h_c}+\epsilon\frac{N}{K}\right\}.
\]

An all-zero signal gives random fishing. The example uses `knowledge_sd = 0.25`;
annual errors and within-year density updates follow A3.

If \(n_c=Nr_c\) with constant relative spatial proportions \(r_c\),
accurate-targeting and random-fishing expectations are proportional to N. Permuting
cells does not change those expectations. Since error SD scales with initial
mean density, a proportionally scaled population also has a proportionally
scaled noisy signal distribution, before depletion. Thus movement alone need not break proportionality. Changing concentration or
knowledge quality can change the location-weighted density in either direction.
The default population and spatial processes impose neither a steady decline
nor a particular CPUE pattern.

Annual simulated CPUE also reflects finite operations and within-year depletion;
the first-operation equation explains the mechanism, not an exact annual fit.
Both scenarios use equal annual effort with inactive quota and mortality caps.
Their replicate variation is conditional on one population, not empirical uncertainty.
